paper_context.research_question: What is the mathematical formalism and theoretical justification for compositionality, particularly additive compositionality, in Skip-Gram word vectors, under what conditions does it hold, what is the correct composition operator when it doesn't, and how does Skip-Gram relate to information-theoretically optimal embedding models like Sufficient Dimensionality Reduction (SDR)?
main_claims: A mathematical formalism for compositionality is provided, defining a 'synonym' based on KL-divergence minimization.
Additive compositionality in Skip-Gram word vectors is theoretically justified under specific assumptions (A1, A2, and uniform word frequency).
Under these assumptions, additive compositionality holds in a stricter sense (small distance rather than small angle).
The success of vector calculus for solving word analogies is explained as a corollary of linear compositionality.
When the uniform word frequency assumption does not hold, compositionality is non-additive, and a non-linear composition operator is provided.
A connection is established between the Skip-Gram model and the Sufficient Dimensionality Reduction (SDR) framework.
Skip-Gram model parameters can be modified to obtain SDR model parameters by adding symbol frequency information (Theorem 3).
This implies that Skip-Gram essentially learns information-theoretically optimal word embeddings in the sense of Globerson and Tishby.
Heuristics commonly used to fit Skip-Gram models can be used to efficiently approximate SDR model parameters.

Clarity and novelty of the proposed mathematical formalism for compositionality.
Plausibility and implications of the assumptions (A1, A2, uniform word frequency) for compositionality.

supporting_evidence: A natural way of capturing the compositionality of words is to say that the set of context words c1, . . . , cm has the same meaning as the single word c if for every other word w, p(w|c1, . . . , cm) = p(w|c) .

Although this is an intuitively satisfying definition, we never expect it to hold exactly; instead, we replace exact equality with the minimization of KL-divergence. identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The 'meaning' of a word is captured by 'the company it keeps', implying that word similarity can be inferred from co-occurrence statistics.
supporting_evidence: A key insight in that regard is to posit that the meaning of a word is captured by “the company it keeps” (Firth, 1957) and, therefore, that two words that keep company with similar words are likely to be similar themselves.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If word meaning is not adequately captured by co-occurrence patterns, the foundational premise for word embeddings and their compositionality, as explored in this work, would be weakened.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Minimizing the angle between context vectors is a good proxy for projecting the theoretical synonym vector onto words in the vocabulary, and this empirically successful approach is justified by the similarity of peaks in categorical distributions.
supporting_evidence: In both cases, we thus need to project the vector(s) onto words in our vocabulary in some manner.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript presents a rigorous theoretical analysis of compositionality in Skip-Gram word embeddings and establishes a novel connection to Sufficient Dimensionality Reduction (SDR) models. The logical flow is well-structured, moving from a general mathematical formalism for compositionality to specific conditions under which additive compositionality holds for Skip-Gram. It then transitions to demonstrating Skip-Gram's information-theoretic optimality by linking it to SDR. The paper clearly states its assumptions and provides proofs for its main theorems, enhancing its logical coherence. While the practical applicability of the general non-additive operator is acknowledged as challenging, and the uniform word frequency assumption for additive compositionality is noted as unrealistic, these limitations are explicitly discussed, maintaining transparency. The work's strength lies in its systematic derivation and the significant theoretical implications for understanding Skip-Gram's success.

Section 2 introduces a mathematical formalism for compositionality by defining a 'synonym' as minimizing KL-divergence (C1, A4).
This formalism is applied to models satisfying assumptions A1 (exponential parametrization of p(w|c)) and A2 (factorization of p(w|C)).
Lemma 1 demonstrates that the Skip-Gram model satisfies A1 and A2 (C3).
Theorem 1 derives a general (non-additive) composition operator for models satisfying A1 and A2 (C2).

Theorem 2 proves that under A1, A2, and A3, compositionality becomes additive (C4).
The success of word analogy solving via vector algebra is explained as a corollary of this linear compositionality (C5).
The paper acknowledges that when A3 does not hold, the compositionality is non-additive, requiring the more complex operator from Theorem 1 (C6).
A practical consideration for projecting theoretical synonyms onto the vocabulary is discussed, justifying angle minimization (A6).
Section 3 shifts focus to the optimality of Skip-Gram embeddings by connecting them to the SDR framework (C7).
Lemma 2 shows that Skip-Gram minimizes a specific KL-divergence objective related to conditional distributions (C11).
Theorem 3 proves that Skip-Gram parameters can be augmented with frequency information to obtain SDR model parameters (C7).
This connection implies that Skip-Gram essentially learns information-theoretically optimal word embeddings (C8, C10).
Consequently, existing Skip-Gram heuristics can be used to efficiently approximate SDR model parameters (C9).

It establishes conditions under which additive compositionality holds for Skip-Gram (SG) models, specifically under assumptions of exponential parametrization (A1), conditional independence of contexts (A2), and crucially, uniform word frequency (A3). When A3 does not hold, the paper derives a general non-additive composition operator. A significant contribution is the theoretical connection between the Skip-Gram model and the Sufficient Dimensionality Reduction (SDR) framework, demonstrating that SG essentially learns information-theoretically optimal word embeddings (in the sense of Globerson and Tishby) by showing how SG parameters can be augmented to yield SDR parameters. This connection provides a strong theoretical justification for the utility of SG embeddings, even when the model's specific assumptions might be misspecified, and suggests that SG's approximation heuristics can be leveraged for SDR.

The paper presents a rigorous mathematical formalism for compositionality in word embeddings, defining a 'synonym' based on KL-divergence minimization. It establishes conditions under which additive compositionality holds for Skip-Gram (SG) models, specifically under assumptions of exponential parametrization (A1), conditional independence of contexts (A2), and crucially, uniform word frequency (A3). This connection provides a strong theoretical justification for the utility of SG embeddings, even when the model's specific assumptions might be misspecified, and suggests that SG's approximation heuristics can be leveraged for SDR.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper provides a robust mathematical formalism for compositionality in word embeddings, defining a 'synonym' through KL-divergence minimization. It rigorously derives a general non-additive composition operator (Theorem 1) applicable to models satisfying assumptions A1 and A2, which the Skip-Gram (SG) model is shown to satisfy under certain conditions (Lemma 1). Additive compositionality (Theorem 2) is theoretically justified for SG under the additional, albeit unrealistic, assumption of uniform word frequency (A3), which then explains the success of vector calculus in word analogies (C5). When A3 does not hold, the paper correctly identifies the composition operator as non-additive (C6). A significant and well-supported contribution is the establishment of a direct connection between Skip-Gram and the Sufficient Dimensionality Reduction (SDR) framework (Theorem 3), demonstrating that SG essentially learns information-theoretically optimal word embeddings (C8) and that SG heuristics can approximate SDR parameters (C9). This connection also implies a robustness of SG's optimality regardless of its specific distributional assumptions (C10). All claims are well-supported by the provided theorems, lemmas, and their proofs within the manuscript, with explicit acknowledgment of the limitations of certain assumptions by the authors themselves.

A natural way of capturing the compositionality of words is to say that the set of context words c1, . . . , cm has the same meaning as the single word c if for every other word w, p(w|c1, . . . , cm) = p(w|c).

Instead, we replace exact equality with the minimization of KL-divergence. That is, we state that the best candidate for having the same meaning as the set of context words C is the word arg min c∈V DKL(p(·|C) | p(·|c)) . (4)
We refer to any vector that minimizes (4) as a synonym of the set of words C.

Summary:
This paper presents a rigorous theoretical analysis of compositionality in Skip-Gram word embeddings, introducing a novel mathematical formalism based on KL-divergence minimization. It systematically derives conditions under which additive compositionality holds for Skip-Gram (specifically, under assumptions A1, A2, and uniform word frequency), and provides a general non-additive operator when these conditions are not met. A significant contribution is the establishment of a direct, provable connection between the Skip-Gram model and the Sufficient Dimensionality Reduction (SDR) framework, demonstrating that Skip-Gram essentially learns information-theoretically optimal word embeddings. This connection re-frames Skip-Gram's empirical success and suggests that its efficient heuristics can be leveraged for approximating SDR model parameters. The work is praised for its mathematical rigor and transparency regarding limitations.

Strengths:
- The paper introduces a clear and rigorous mathematical formalism for compositionality based on KL-divergence minimization, providing a solid theoretical foundation.
- A strong theoretical justification for Skip-Gram's information-theoretic optimality is established through its novel and direct connection to the Sufficient Dimensionality Reduction (SDR) framework.
- The work logically progresses from a general non-additive composition operator to a specific additive operator, clearly delineating the conditions under which each applies.
- The authors are transparent in acknowledging the unrealistic nature of the uniform word frequency assumption for additive compositionality and the computational challenges of the non-linear operator.
- The paper provides a formal theoretical explanation for the empirically observed success of vector calculus in solving word analogies.

Limitations:
1. The derivation of additive compositionality (Theorem 2) relies on the assumption of uniform word frequency (A3), which the authors explicitly state is 'not realistic' for natural language corpora. This significantly limits the direct applicability of additive compositionality as a general phenomenon in real-world Skip-Gram embeddings without corpus manipulation.
2. The practical implementation of the general non-additive composition operator (Theorem 1) requires solving a 'highly nonlinear system of equations', posing a significant computational challenge and limiting its practical utility compared to simpler linear methods.
3. The 'optimality' of Skip-Gram embeddings, derived from the SDR connection (C8, C10), is specifically defined within an information-theoretic framework (maximal mutual information preservation). This specific definition of optimality may not directly translate to superior performance across all diverse empirical NLP tasks, requiring careful contextualization.
4. The scope of assumption A2 for Skip-Gram is limited to cases where the number of composed words (m) is less than or equal to the window size (∆). The implications for compositionality when 'm > ∆' are not explicitly addressed, potentially limiting the applicability of the derived formalism for longer compositional phrases.
5. The foundational definition of compositionality via KL-divergence minimization (A4) is an operational choice. Its complete alignment with human cognitive models of semantic compositionality, or its superiority over other potential metrics, is an underlying assumption that could be further explored or contextualized.
6. The practical step of projecting the theoretical synonym vector onto an actual word in the vocabulary by minimizing the angle (A6) is noted as an empirical heuristic rather than a direct, theoretically derived projection method, potentially introducing a gap between the theoretical ideal and practical implementation.

Open Questions:
1. How might the practical implications of the uniform word frequency assumption (A3) be addressed, perhaps by linking it to corpus preprocessing techniques (e.g., subsampling) or quantifying the deviation from additivity under more realistic distributions?
2. Can the authors explore potential approximation methods or heuristics for efficiently solving the non-linear system of equations required by the general composition operator (Theorem 1), or provide a more detailed analysis of its computational feasibility?

6. Given that angle minimization for projecting theoretical synonyms onto the vocabulary is an empirical heuristic (A6), could the authors acknowledge this more explicitly and discuss the potential for discrepancies between the theoretically optimal synonym and the word identified by this proxy, or suggest avenues for a more theoretically grounded projection?

Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 5. Check that your scores reflect the review I3
Codes: I3
Applies To: meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: Starting with February 2025, ARR reviewers are asked to provide three scores: soundness, excitement, and overall recommendation. I3 The soundness scores must be justified by the text of the review . If you give a low Soundness score without finding any major faults, this means that your review is not a faithful explanation of your recommendation, and you need to revise it. One possible reason for low soundness scores without sufficient justification could be reliance on some unconscious bias or heuristic, like the ones listed in the previous section. Likewise, low reproducibility scores should be justified. Sometimes you may find the work sound, but not something that is interesting for you personally. Such preferences are more subjective and should be reflected in a separate excitement score, which is orthogonal to the assessment of the soundness of the paper. Excitement scores reflect our personal taste, and so do not necessarily come with explicit reasons. The Overall assessment score is an explicit recommendation for the outcome of this paper, if it were committed to an *ACL venue. This is a composite score reflecting your assessment of soundness, excitement, and also other factors like novelty and impact. All papers recommended for Findings and main conferences are expected to be sufficiently sound and reproducible, but you may consider a paper worthy of the main conference even if you personally are not excited about it.

Introduction The distributional hypothesis states that words that occur in similar contexts are se- mantically similar. The claim has multiple theoretical roots in psychology, structuralist lin- guistics, lexicography and possibly even in the later writings of Wittgenstein (Firth, 1957; Harris, 1954; Miller & Charles, 1991; Wittgenstein, 1953). Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.
